headline: DEA rescheduling briefs close; judge's Schedule III call is next
dek: The DEA and its opponents filed final replies on 5 November over a GAO report, ending the stay and leaving Judge Derek Julius free to write his recommendation.
key_points: The DEA and three anti-rescheduling parties filed their last reply briefs on 5 November, the final scheduled round of written argument in the Schedule III hearing.
The fight was over a 23 September GAO report finding that DEA and FDA lack written procedures for scheduling reviews; the DEA says it deserves no weight.
With the deadline passed, the stay has expired and Chief Administrative Law Judge Derek Julius can issue his recommendation, though no deadline binds him.
His recommendation is not binding: parties can contest it before DEA Administrator Terry Cole makes the final decision.
body: The paper fight over whether marijuana belongs in Schedule III is finished. On Thursday, 5 November, the Drug Enforcement Administration and the three parties opposing the move filed their final reply briefs, closing the last scheduled round of written argument in the administrative hearing that began in June.

That matters because it removes the procedural brake that has held the case since late September. With the 5 November deadline passed, the temporary stay has expired, according to The Marijuana Herald, and Chief Administrative Law Judge Derek Julius can now turn to the recommendation he will send to DEA Administrator Terry Cole. No deadline has been set, so it could come at any time, or not for weeks.
## What the last round was about

The final briefs were narrow by design. On 23 September the Government Accountability Office published a report on how federal drug scheduling works. It found that the DEA has no written policies setting out how its staff should evaluate or schedule substances, and that the Food and Drug Administration has no written procedures for how its staff build scheduling recommendations. The agencies agreed with GAO's recommendations to write some.

Three parties that took part in the hearing as opponents, the National Drug & Alcohol Screening Association, DUID Victim Voices and physician Kenneth Finn, seized on the report. They asked the judge to reopen the hearing for new testimony and document discovery. On 22 October Julius said no to that, but he admitted the report into the record and allowed short briefs on how much weight it should carry, with opening briefs due 29 October and replies due 5 November.
## The DEA: no new information

The DEA's six-page reply asked the judge to give the GAO report no weight at all. Its core argument, as described by Marijuana Moment and The Marijuana Herald, is that the opponents are using the report to re-argue points already tested over the summer, and that a document about missing paperwork says nothing about the science.

The agency also turned the opponents' logic back on them. The same lack of written internal guidelines existed in 2016, when federal reviewers recommended keeping marijuana in Schedule I, a result the opponents defend. If the absence of written procedures spoils the current review, the DEA argued, it would spoil that one too. In its words, the opponents "cannot have it both ways."

The DEA added that the opponents had not engaged with the large body of scientific and medical evidence presented at the hearing. In its earlier post-hearing brief, the agency said more than 30,000 practitioners treat over six million patients across 43 US jurisdictions, and asked the judge to recommend Schedule III promptly.
## The opponents: a test chosen in a black box

The opponents' seven-page joint reply argued that the GAO findings go to the heart of the case, not its paperwork. Their main target is the two-part test federal officials used to decide that marijuana has a currently accepted medical use, which replaced an older five-part test. A 2024 Justice Department Office of Legal Counsel opinion called the old test impermissibly narrow.

According to the brief, FDA began evaluating marijuana in late 2022 but was formally directed to use the new test only in July 2023, after much of the work was done. They point to hearing testimony that marijuana would not have passed the old test. Without written procedures, they say, nobody can show why the new test was chosen or who chose it, so the government cannot carry its burden of proof. They asked Julius to recommend that Cole reject rescheduling on the existing record.
> The briefs are done; what's left is a judgment call by one judge, then by one administrator.
## What the GAO report does and doesn't say

Both sides are leaning hard on a document that is more limited than either framing suggests. The report did not find the marijuana proposal unlawful and did not assess whether marijuana belongs in Schedule III, The Marijuana Herald and Cannabis News noted. It also found that across 95 substances requiring HHS evaluations from 2020 through 2025, the DEA considered HHS input every time, and its final decisions matched HHS recommendations for all 84 that had a final rule by the end of 2025.
That record cuts in the DEA's favour on consistency. The opponents' answer is that consistency without written rules is still unreviewable. The judge will decide which reading carries more weight.
## Where this sits in the bigger picture

This hearing covers the broad question of moving all marijuana to Schedule III. A narrower change already happened: in April, Attorney General Todd Blanche ordered state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved marijuana products into Schedule III immediately. That order is what made the DEA's new registration system for medical businesses possible, which we covered on 6 November as the agency listed more than 900 registered dispensaries.

Separately, challengers have consolidated lawsuits against the April order in the US Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, where a proposed briefing schedule runs into early 2027. So even a favourable recommendation from Julius would not end the legal contest.

The politics have also moved. After the midterms, a senior adviser to President Trump said the president would sign a clean descheduling bill, as we reported on 6 November. Congressional Cannabis Caucus co-chair Rep. Dina Titus told Marijuana Moment she would urge him to sign such legislation.
## What to watch

First, the recommendation itself. It will set the tone for everything that follows, and its treatment of the two-part medical-use test will matter more than any other single finding. Second, the exceptions period: parties can challenge the judge's findings before the file reaches Cole. Third, Cole's final rule, which would then face the same kind of court challenge the April order already has. For operators, the stakes now reach beyond the medical businesses covered by April's order to the whole state-licensed adult-use market, and that still depends on a final rule that survives review.
